parent.name: Polish Opening
parent.overview: White plays 1.b4 to grab queenside space and fianchetto the bishop to b2, putting long-diagonal pressure on e5, f6 and g7. It is an irregular flank opening: Black chooses the set-up with 1...e5 (2.Bb2 Bxb4 3.Bxe5, the Exchange Variation, which equalises), 1...d5 (the German Defence 2...Qd6 etc.), or 1...Nf6 and 1...e6 reaching Indian-like or Queen's Gambit-like set-ups. The opening is sound and not refuted but gives Black no real problems, so it is rarely seen at elite level and chosen as a surprise weapon (Carlsen used it against Nakamura and So in 2021). Theory is small and the play is flank-oriented, with unbalanced pawn structures but typically no early forced tactics. Alekhine's complaint was that it reveals White's intentions before knowing Black's.

parent.name: Pirc Defense
parent.overview: Black plays 1...d6 and, after 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3, ...g6 and ...Bg7, letting White build the broad e4-d4 centre and then undermining it from the flanks with ...c5 or ...e5 (hypermodern: the bigger White's centre, the bigger the target). The root is a crossroads: 1...d6 can transpose to the Philidor (3...e5 or ...c6) or to the Modern. White's replies run from sharp (Austrian Attack 4.f4, 150 Attack 4.Be3 with Qd2, Bh6 and h4-h5, Byrne 4.Bg5, Bayonet h4) to unhurried (Classical 4.Nf3 with Be2 and castling, fianchetto). Typical play is imbalanced: White gets space and often a kingside attack, Black gets a solid fianchettoed king and counterplay on the queenside and with central breaks. It is sound but has a reputation for giving White chances; Kasparov doubted it for the top level (s1), though Caruana, Anand and Grischuk have used it (s2).

parent.name: Caro-Kann Defense
parent.overview: Black plays ...c6 to support ...d5 and so challenges the e4 pawn with a sound pawn structure, while keeping the light-squared bishop free to come out to f5 or g4 before ...e6 (the French Defence's main drawback, at the cost of a tempo). Black accepts less space early and tends to get a resilient, hard-to-break structure with few weaknesses and good endgame prospects. Play is mostly positional and manoeuvring; it is called more solid and less dynamic than the Sicilian (s1). The Advance (3.e5 Bf5) and Panov-Botvinnik (3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4) lines are more combative, and the Advance became the most popular White try in the 21st century. Main branches: Classical (4...Bf5), Advance, Exchange, Panov, 4...Nf6 lines, Gurgenidze (...g6), Two Knights (2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3) and Fantasy (3.f3). This is a crossroads root after 1...c6; the pawn structures differ by branch.

parent.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Queen's Knight Variation
parent.overview: The QGD with 3.Nc3 develops the knight and adds pressure on d5. The usual continuation is 3...Nf6, after which White chooses 4.Bg5 (pin; Black replies Orthodox 4...Be7, Cambridge Springs, Tartakower ...b6 or Lasker ...Ne4), 4.Nf3 or the Exchange 4.cxd5. Black holds d5 with ...e6, which gives a bulletproof centre but locks the c8 bishop; Black frees the game with ...c5 or ...e5, or ...b6 and ...Bb7. White's main plans are the minority attack (b4-b5 against c6) in Exchange structures, or central play with e4. Play is slow and technical rather than tactical, with a strong reputation for soundness, and the Cambridge Springs is the one trappy tactical sub-line.

parent.name: Old Indian Defense
parent.overview: The Old Indian (1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6, here reached by 1.d4 d6 2.c4) is the pre-fianchetto cousin of the King's Indian. Black sets up ...d6, ...e5, ...Nbd7, ...Be7, ...O-O and ...c6, aiming at a Philidor-like central structure that is solid and defensible but a little cramped. The main line is the Ukrainian Variation 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nf3 Nbd7 5.e4 Be7 6.Be2 O-O 7.O-O c6 8.Re1, where theory considers White slightly better. It has never been as popular as the King's Indian; the bishop on e7 is less active than a fianchetto. King's Indian players use it to sidestep the Samisch and Averbakh. The data root also holds the Neo-Old Indian / Modern set-up (1.d4 d6 2.c4 g6), which transposes to King's Indian or Pirc-like structures.

parent.name: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Rubinstein System
parent.moves: 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Bb4 4. e3
parent.overview: White ignores the pin and the threat of ...Bxc3+ and develops with Bd3, Nf3, O-O (or Ne2), accepting that doubled c-pawns may arise and banking on the bishop pair and central space; the e4 square is the recurring battleground. Black chooses between 4...O-O (flexible; 5.Bd3 d5 6.Nf3 c5 is the main line), 4...c5 (immediate pressure on d4; Hübner-style 5.Ne2 lines where White avoids doubled pawns) and 4...b6 (St. Petersburg, controlling e4 with ...Bb7). Typical middlegames feature central tension and a pawn-structure battle: hanging pawns on c3/d4 which Black blockades with knights on c4/d5, an isolated d4-pawn for White after ...cxd4 exd4, or a closed knight-versus-bishops game in the Hübner. Play is positional and manoeuvring, with understanding of the structures more important than memorised sequences.

parent.name: King's Indian Defense: Normal Variation
parent.moves: 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 g6 3. Nc3 Bg7 4. e4 d6
parent.overview: This root is the King's Indian reached by the move order 1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.c4 (the same position as 3.Nf3 in the 2.c4 move order). It is not a distinct opening: it is the ordinary King's Indian, where Black fianchettoes with ...Bg7, castles, and strikes at White's centre with ...e5, ...c5 or ...f5. White's choice of set-up decides the character: the classical 4.Nc3 and e4 leads to the locked-centre opposite-wing race (c4-c5 against ...f5-f4), while the Fianchetto Variation (g3, Bg2, O-O, Nc3) is quieter, positional, and has less forcing theory. The data subtree groups 4.e4 Normal Variation lines (the majority of games) under this root, so it mixes both. Black's success depends on timing and coordination rather than automatic aggression.
